exercise1.prompt: CSV Options That Matter: Count the rows in a tab-separated file

files.scores.tsv:
name	score
a	1
b	2
c	3
d	4

exercise1.hint: Without sep="\t" the whole line lands in one column and you get one column and three rows — the row count would look right and the table would be wrong. len(df) or df.shape[0] counts the rows.

exercise2.prompt: CSV Options That Matter: A file with no header

hiddenCases.name: a two-row file gives two rows
a one-row file is not read as header only
pandas does the reading
hiddenCases.describe: pd.read_csv rather than the answer typed in

exercise2.hint: Supplying names= tells pandas there is no header to read. Reading it with neither argument takes your first row of data as the column names, and the count comes back one short.

questions.prompt: A file separates fields with tabs. Which argument do you need?
questions.explain: Without it the whole line lands in one column, and the load succeeds while the table is wrong.

choices: Removes the header from the file
Stops the first row being read as column names
Raises if there is a header
questions.explain: Without it, your first row of real data becomes the header and you are quietly one row short.

questions.prompt: You loaded a six-column file and shape says (1000, 1). What is the likely cause?
questions.explain: Each line arrived unsplit as a single value. The shape said so before any of the numbers did.

questions.prompt: An export has a title line and a blank line above the header. What handles it?
questions.explain: skiprows steps over the junk so the real header is where pandas expects it.
